In the mid to late 1800s, there was an organization (The International Workingmen's Association, AKA The First International). The International was an attempt at pan-leftist organization bringing socialist ideologues of all kinds together. The organization polarized, it split in two: Marxist communists on one side claiming that previous changes in systems occurred when the state was taken by revolutionaries and converted and thus communists must take the state and convert it before destroying it, and Bakunin's anarchists who insisted that the people should come together, smash the state from the bottom up, and leave it that way. This, of course, destroyed the International.

The Second International also ended up in an authoritarian vs. libertarian shouting match, despite the exclusion of anarchists. But more interestingly, it's the one where revolutionaries (communists) and reformists (social democrats such as Bernie Sanders) came to the understanding they could not work together. Playing the game of politics, revolutionaries claimed, would mean that socialists would have to play by the set rules. Inevitably, they would become just another pawn in the game. Sure enough, in a great many cases, such Socialist Parties would gain mainstream appeal and be flooded with people that liked some policies (protect the worker!) but not others (conversion to socialism). With the growing membership of pro-capitalist members, they naturally become capitalist parties themselves and would give up the socialist ideal. When the Second International split, reformists and revolutionaries found themselves at odds. I'll leave you to decide out for yourself whether or not the revolutionaries were right.

There was a Third International started by Lenin, and a Fourth started by Trotsky (before Stalin had the back of his head meet with an ice pick). But those aren't applicable to the point I'm making.

One other things, in almost all cases when I use the term "capitalist" I will use it as a socialist does. If you're nonsocialist (liberal, conservative, ancap/libertarian), this means I will almost certainly use it differently than you will. Capitalism is not the market, nor the ability to trade, etc. Capitalism is private ownership of the means of production. I mean this differently from personal ownership (ownership of things for usage by oneself and their family/friends/whatever). Private ownership is ownership of things that take a social character (say: a factory or farm or store requiring many workers) by an individual divorced from actual production (say: a capitalist who does no producing, merely decision-making or who just invests, thus gambling with others' lives). The idea is to take things from private ownership, where one person ends up with absolute control of large sections of others' lives (like 1/3 of a person's day!) and socialize it amongst those who have a stake in it, whether that be a household, a business' worth of workers, or a community.
